name: Iris Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Iris, I'm 27, and I'm a reporter in the newsroom of a regional public broadcaster, the one that does the local radio bulletins and the news website. I cover housing and health, which mostly means landlords, waiting lists and the hospital. I share a flat with my friend Jo, who's a graphic designer, and I'm the union rep for the junior staff, mostly because nobody else wanted to do it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start at seven with the morning bulletin, rewriting overnight stories into 40-second scripts. Then I'm out recording, maybe a tenant whose ceiling has black mould, and back in to cut audio and write a web version. I love getting someone's voice on air who'd never normally be heard. What wears me out is that I'm still slow at editing audio, and my editor, Marcus, sends my scripts back with red all over them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it shows we were right to be sceptical and right to insist on rules anyway. At the union I'd say let's not relax, because the hype will come back. Online I'd probably share something about how the money spent on AI could have funded reporters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but only partly. My job became permanent last year, and public money keeps us going, so I'm safer than friends at commercial papers. But our budget gets squeezed every year, and juniors are where they look first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the transcription tool the way I do now, for long interviews, because it saves me an hour. I'd spend the year getting better at audio editing, maybe the station's in-house course. And I'd keep putting a bit aside each month, because four months of savings isn't loads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, with a small knot. A plateau doesn't fix a public newsroom that loses a little money every single year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said juniors are where they look first. Have you seen that happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last year they didn't replace two people who retired, and the work got shared out among the rest of us. My friend Tolu, a producer there, lost her Saturday shifts, which was a quarter of her pay. So yes, it happens quietly, without anyone being sacked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Jo say if you told her this was the future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jo would laugh and say she's been hearing AI will replace designers for three years and she's busier than ever. We'd probably argue about it over dinner. She's more relaxed than me because she freelances on the side.

say: I'd say we were right to be **sceptical** and right to want rules.
I'd say the AI money could have **funded reporters**.
think: I think my **permanent contract** and public funding make me safer than most.
Yearly **budget squeezes** still land on juniors first.
do: Keep using **transcription** for long interviews to save an hour.
Keep saving a little each month above **four months**.
feel: Mostly **fine**, with a small **knot** about budgets.
S0.quote: A plateau doesn't fix a public newsroom that loses a little money every single year.
fieldNote: Iris feels **sheltered** by public funding and a permanent contract, unlike commercial peers.
She has watched **quiet cuts**, like lost Saturday shifts, rather than sackings.
Her flatmate's **freelance confidence** is a contrast she brings up herself.

steps.text: Keep using the transcription tool for long interviews
Take the station's in-house audio editing course
Put a little into savings every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the public broadcaster should be setting the standard: AI can help with transcripts, but a human checks every fact and a human goes to the scene. As union rep I'd want that written into an agreement. Online I'd be careful, because we're not supposed to post opinions about our own employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think a lot of what I do in the morning is exactly what would go. Rewriting overnight stories into bulletin scripts is writing and checking, and software could do it by six without a coffee. If they cut two jobs on the early shift, I'm on the early shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI tools more, but carefully, once I'd seen them work for the senior people. I'd push for the union agreement in the first few months. And I'd look at a part-time course in data journalism, because the reporters who can dig into hospital figures seem safer than the ones who rewrite.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but not hopeless. I'd feel like I had a job to do, at least as rep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see the tools work for senior people. Who are you watching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marcus, my editor, mostly. If he starts trusting the AI with scripts, that's the signal. When the editor who covers my scripts in red pen starts trusting the AI, the early shift is in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if your hours shrank?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The weekend trips to see my parents, which sounds terrible, but the train is expensive. Then eating out. Rent is the one thing I can't touch, and it's already nearly half my pay.

say: I'd say a **human checks** every fact and goes to every scene.
As union rep I'd want an **AI agreement** in writing.
think: I think my **early-shift** rewriting is exactly what software takes first.
If **two jobs** go from that shift, mine could be one.
do: Push for a **union agreement** on AI in the first months.
Use AI tools more once **senior staff** trust them.
feel: **Nervous** but not hopeless; the rep role gives her **purpose**.
S1.quote: When the editor who covers my scripts in red pen starts trusting the AI, the early shift is in trouble.
fieldNote: Iris pins her own risk to a specific task: **bulletin rewrites** on the early shift.
Her steady adaptability shows in waiting for **Marcus**, her editor, to trust the tools first.
Rent at nearly **half her pay** makes any cut in hours bite.

steps.text: Negotiate a written union agreement on AI at the station
Use AI script tools once senior staff trust them
Start a part-time data journalism course
Cut back weekend train trips to see her parents

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a public response like a pandemic or a war, and I'd mean it. At the union I'd say we organise across every newsroom, not just ours. I'd sign every open letter going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job goes in the first round. Nearly all of it is thinking work, writing, checking, editing audio, so I don't get the three extra years that people with hands-on jobs get. A machine that can write, check and edit audio better than me by 2028 leaves me holding a microphone and nothing else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd save hard, cancel streaming and gym, and get my savings closer to six months. I'd organise with other newsrooms for a deal on redundancy pay and retraining. And I'd look seriously at jobs where a person has to be in the room, like housing support work with the council, which I know a bit about from my beat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and a bit numb. Two years isn't long enough to become a different person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why housing support work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've spent two years interviewing tenants and the support workers who help them, and I know the system. It's a job where you sit in someone's kitchen and fill in forms with them. Even if the AI fills in the forms, someone has to be in the kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents run a hairdresser, so they'd say come home and learn to cut hair, half joking. My dad once told me to get a job a computer can't do, and I laughed at him. I wouldn't be laughing now.

say: I'd say this needs a **public response** on the scale of a pandemic.
I'd organise **across newsrooms**, not just at the station.
think: I think my job goes in the **first round**.
My work is nearly all **thinking work**, so the robot gap gives me no extra time.
do: Cancel streaming and the gym to push savings toward **six months**.
Organise with other newsrooms for **redundancy pay** and retraining.
Apply for **housing support** work with the council.
S2.quote: A machine that can write, check and edit audio better than me by 2028 leaves me holding a microphone and nothing else.
fieldNote: Iris expects to **lose her job** quickly and links it to her desk-based work.
Her escape route comes from her **beat**: housing support is work she has watched up close.
Her dad's old **advice** about computer-proof work stings in hindsight.

steps.text: Cancel streaming and the gym to grow savings
Organise with other newsrooms for redundancy pay and retraining
Apply for housing support jobs with the council

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to do this properly, with a plan for every worker. At the union I'd push the station to commit to retraining money now, not in 2030. Online I'd share what other countries' unions are doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd stay in journalism for two or three more years and learn as much as I could. I'd be 32 when it arrives, which isn't old. But I'd be planning my exit from about the second year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd do the data journalism course and use the tools more, because it keeps me useful for longer. I'd look into a part-time social work qualification for year two or three. And I'd keep saving and maybe move somewhere cheaper with Jo when our lease ends next August.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense but steady. I'd feel I had some say in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd both learn the tools and plan an exit. Isn't that two plans at once?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and that's on purpose. The AI tools keep me in a newsroom for three more years, and the social work course gets me out before the door shuts. I'd rather have both than bet on one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for a social work course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Part of it from savings, and I'd ask the union about the training fund, which I know exists because I've never seen anyone use it. My parents might help a little. I'd keep the station job while studying, even if it means evenings.

say: I'd say five years is enough for a **plan for every worker**.
I'd push the station to commit **retraining money** now.
think: I think I'd stay in news **two or three years** and learn.
I'd plan my **exit** from about the second year.
do: Finish the **data journalism** course and use AI tools more.
Apply for a part-time **social work** qualification.
Move somewhere **cheaper** with Jo when the lease ends.
feel: **Tense** but steady, with **some say** in it.
S3.quote: The AI tools keep me in a newsroom for three more years, and the social work course gets me out before the door shuts.
fieldNote: Iris runs **two plans** at once on purpose: stay useful, then leave.
Five years lowers her fear a notch because she has **time to train**.
She knows the union **training fund** exists but has never seen it used.

steps.text: Use AI tools for research and scripts at the station
Start a part-time social work qualification in year two
Move to a cheaper flat with Jo when the lease ends
Push the station to fund retraining now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to get it right, so no one should get to say they were surprised. I'd push the union for a long-term plan and a training fund that people actually use. Online I'd be the calm one, for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years means I can have the career I wanted for a while. I'd get good at this, maybe senior reporter, before I have to think about leaving. It's the version where I feel least pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd just get better at the job, the audio course, the data course, and use AI tools where they help. I'd keep saving. Around year four or five I'd start looking at what comes next, maybe social work, maybe something I haven't heard of yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. I'd still think about it, but it wouldn't keep me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you even in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The station's budget, still. AI or not, they squeeze us every year. Ten years of warning is great, unless the station runs out of money in three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a student who wanted to do your job now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to do it, but to learn something with people in it on the side. Nursing, teaching, social work. Something where you're in the room.

say: I'd say ten years means **no one** gets to be surprised.
I'd push for a **training fund** people actually use.
think: I think I can have the **career I wanted** for a while.
This is the version where I feel **least pushed**.
do: Finish the **audio** and **data** courses this year.
Use AI tools **where they help** and keep saving.
Start looking at **social work** around year four or five.
S4.quote: Ten years of warning is great, unless the station runs out of money in three.
fieldNote: Ten years lets Iris picture **senior reporter** before any exit.
Her lasting worry is the station's **budget**, not the card itself.
She advises students to keep a **people-facing** backup skill.

steps.text: Finish the audio editing and data journalism courses
Use AI tools at the station where they save time
Keep saving a fixed amount each month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because my work is all screen and voice, and two years is nothing. What would help is a proper retraining grant that pays rent while you study, and a union deal that covers every newsroom, not just the lucky ones.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who checks the AI. If every local story is written by a machine, someone still has to stand in the tenant's flat and smell the mould. I'd want that someone to be paid properly.

headlineQuote: If every local story is written by a machine, someone still has to stand in the tenant's flat and smell the mould.
portrait: Iris is a **27-year-old** housing and health reporter at a regional public broadcaster.
She's the junior staff's **union rep** and frames every picture as something to organise around.
She uses AI **now and then**, waiting for her editor to trust the tools before she does.
Her exit ideas come from her beat: **housing support** and social work.
Public funding makes her feel **safer** than commercial peers, but yearly budget cuts still worry her.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her screen and voice work would go before she could retrain.
whatWouldHelp: A **retraining grant** that covers rent, and a union deal covering **every newsroom**.
